scenes.teachingReason: A budget is a plan. Monitoring is checking whether you stuck to it, regularly. For each category, the variance is the actual spending minus the budget. Say one week you spent ninety-two eating out, against sixty. That's plus thirty-two, overspent. Entertainment was thirty-one, against forty, minus nine. Clothes were on budget, and groceries were plus sixteen. Keep the signs and add them, plus thirty-nine dollars. If every week went like that, the surplus would drop to a hundred and ninety-four, and the fund would take thirty-four weeks, not twenty-nine. Small overspends quietly add five weeks. Adding the numbers without their signs gives fifty-seven, which isn't what happened.

scenes.teachingReason: So should the fund be three months, or six? That's a judgement about risk, so back it with numbers. With a steady wage, pay is unlikely to stop suddenly, so three months, six and a half thousand dollars, is a sensible target. With casual or changing hours, pay can drop without warning, and it can take longer to recover. Then six months, about thirteen thousand dollars, is safer, even though it takes fifty-seven weeks to build instead of twenty-nine. A good answer names the situation, and quotes the numbers.

scenes.teachingReason: Put it together, and each strategy answers a different question. A budget asks, can my pay cover my life? Saving first asks, does the saving actually happen? An emergency fund asks, what if a big bill comes, or my pay stops? And monitoring asks, am I sticking to the plan? No single one is enough on its own. So, budget, save first, keep a fund, and check your spending regularly, every week or month.
